# Tutorial 08: The Master Plan — Capital Rationing and the Dean Model

## Exercise 1: The Dean Model at a Craft Brewery

Specht Craft Brewing GmbH wants to grow and has collected four independent project proposals for next year. Its financing options become more expensive the more it raises — Uncle Rüdiger's equity, for example, costs 13% plus a permanent seat at the regulars' table. Treat the model as single-period: each IRR can be compared directly with each financing cost. Amounts in € thousand.

| Project | Description | $I_0$ | IRR $r$ |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| K1 | New brewhouse kettle | 400 | 15% |
| K2 | Canning line | 300 | 12% |
| K3 | Taproom extension | 400 | 9% |
| K4 | Electric delivery vans | 200 | 6% |

| Source | Description | Amount | Cost $k$ |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| F1 | Retained earnings | 300 | 4% |
| F2 | House-bank loan | 600 | 7% |
| F3 | Second bank loan | 400 | 10% |
| F4 | Equity from Uncle Rüdiger | 400 | 13% |

#### Task 1: Build the staircases

Construct the investment staircase and the financing staircase (cumulative volumes) and merge them into one interval table that shows, for each volume interval, the project being funded, the source funding it and the spread between IRR and financing cost.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Investment staircase (sorted by IRR, descending): K1 0–400 (15%), K2 400–700 (12%), K3 700–1,100 (9%), K4 1,100–1,300 (6%).

Financing staircase (sorted by cost, ascending): F1 0–300 (4%), F2 300–900 (7%), F3 900–1,300 (10%), F4 1,300–1,700 (13%).

Merged at all breakpoints (0, 300, 400, 700, 900, 1,100, 1,300):

| Volume (€ thousand) | Project | IRR | Source | Cost | Spread |
|:--:|:--:|--:|:--:|--:|--:|
| 0–300 | K1 | 15% | F1 | 4% | +11 pp |
| 300–400 | K1 | 15% | F2 | 7% | +8 pp |
| 400–700 | K2 | 12% | F2 | 7% | +5 pp |
| 700–900 | K3 | 9% | F2 | 7% | +2 pp |
| 900–1,100 | K3 | 9% | F3 | 10% | −1 pp |
| 1,100–1,300 | K4 | 6% | F3 | 10% | −4 pp |

**Grading Notes:** both staircases correctly sorted; breakpoints from *both* staircases used in the merged table.
:::

#### Task 2: Optimal programme and cut-off rate

Assume that all projects are divisible. Determine the optimal investment programme, the capital budget, the financing mix and the endogenous cut-off rate $i^*$. Explain which of the two intersection cases applies.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

The spread turns negative at a volume of **€900 thousand**, in the middle of K3. At this point the financing staircase jumps vertically from 7% (F2 exhausted) to 10% (F3), while the investment staircase runs flat at 9% (K3). The curves cross on a vertical step of the **financing** staircase, so the cut-off rate equals the IRR of the marginal project:

$$i^* = r_{K3} = 9\%$$

- Programme: K1 and K2 in full, **half of K3** (€200 thousand of €400 thousand); K4 rejected.
- Capital budget: $400 + 300 + 200 = 900$, i.e. **€900 thousand**.
- Financing: F1 €300 thousand and F2 €600 thousand (both fully used); F3 and F4 not used.

Check with the decision rule: K1 and K2 have IRRs above 9%, K4 below; F1 and F2 cost less than 9%, F3 and F4 more.

One-period surplus (spread × volume): $300 \cdot 0.11 + 100 \cdot 0.08 + 300 \cdot 0.05 + 200 \cdot 0.02 = 33 + 8 + 15 + 4 = 60$, i.e. **€60 thousand**.
:::

#### Task 3: The taproom is indivisible

The architect points out that half a taproom is not a taproom: K3 can only be built in full or not at all. Should Specht build it? Compare the one-period surplus (project returns minus interest) with and without the full K3.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

*Without K3* (volume 700, financed by F1 300 and F2 400):

$$\text{Returns} = 400 \cdot 0.15 + 300 \cdot 0.12 = 60 + 36 = 96$$
$$\text{Interest} = 300 \cdot 0.04 + 400 \cdot 0.07 = 12 + 28 = 40$$

Surplus: $96 - 40 = 56$, i.e. **€56 thousand**.

*With the full K3* (volume 1,100, financed by F1 300, F2 600 and F3 200):

$$\text{Returns} = 96 + 400 \cdot 0.09 = 132$$
$$\text{Interest} = 300 \cdot 0.04 + 600 \cdot 0.07 + 200 \cdot 0.10 = 12 + 42 + 20 = 74$$

Surplus: $132 - 74 = 58$, i.e. **€58 thousand**.

Marginal view: the first €200 thousand of K3 earn 2 points more than F2 ($+4$), the second €200 thousand earn 1 point less than F3 ($-2$); net $+2$, i.e. **+€2 thousand**. Specht should build the full taproom and draw €200 thousand from F3. Compared with the divisible optimum (€60 thousand), indivisibility costs €2 thousand.
:::

#### Task 4: The house bank becomes generous

After a good harvest of hop futures, the house bank raises its credit line F2 from €600 thousand to **€1,000 thousand** at 7%; everything else stays the same. Determine the new programme, the capital budget and the new cut-off rate. Why has the cut-off rate changed?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

New financing staircase: F1 0–300 (4%), F2 300–1,300 (7%), F3 1,300–1,700 (10%), …

| Volume (€ thousand) | Project | IRR | Source | Cost | Spread |
|:--:|:--:|--:|:--:|--:|--:|
| 0–300 | K1 | 15% | F1 | 4% | +11 pp |
| 300–400 | K1 | 15% | F2 | 7% | +8 pp |
| 400–700 | K2 | 12% | F2 | 7% | +5 pp |
| 700–1,100 | K3 | 9% | F2 | 7% | +2 pp |
| 1,100–1,300 | K4 | 6% | F2 | 7% | −1 pp |

The spread turns negative at **€1,100 thousand**. Here the investment staircase drops vertically from 9% (K3) to 6% (K4), while the financing staircase runs flat at 7% (F2). The curves now cross on a vertical step of the **investment** staircase, so the cut-off rate equals the cost of the marginal financing source:

$$i^* = k_{F2} = 7\%$$

Programme: K1, K2 and K3 in full; K4 still rejected (6% < 7%). Budget: **€1,100 thousand**, financed by F1 €300 thousand and €800 thousand of the €1,000 thousand F2 line.

The cut-off rate falls from 9% to 7% because more cheap money is available: the internal "price" of capital is endogenous — it reflects the firm's own financing conditions, not a market rate given from outside.
:::

## Exercise 2: A Frozen Budget at the Bakery

Morgenrot Bäckereien GmbH, a regional bakery chain, has been told by its banks that next year's investment budget is capped at **€6.0 million** — hard rationing, served with fresh rolls. Five independent, indivisible projects compete for the money. Each runs for five years with constant annual cash flows at the end of each year and no residual value; the cost of capital is $i = 8\%$.

| Project | Description | $I_0$ (€) | Annual cash flow, $t = 1, \dots, 5$ (€) |
|:--:|:--|--:|--:|
| A | Central bakery oven line | 4,000,000 | 1,150,000 |
| B | Solar roof on the central bakery | 2,500,000 | 760,000 |
| C | Three new branches | 3,500,000 | 1,000,000 |
| D | Electric delivery vans | 1,500,000 | 420,000 |
| E | Café extension in the old town | 6,000,000 | 1,600,000 |

#### Task 1: NPV and Profitability Index

Calculate the NPV and the Profitability Index of each project and rank the projects by PI. Use the factor $PVIFA(8\%, 5) = 3.9927$ from the Formula Collection.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

Timeline of each project: $-I_0$ at $t = 0$, then the same cash flow $CF$ at $t = 1, \dots, 5$ (discounted ←). Present value of the inflows: $PV = CF \cdot PVIFA(8\%, 5) = CF \cdot 3.9927$; then $NPV = PV - I_0$ and $PI = PV / I_0$.

Example project A: $PV = 1{,}150{,}000 \cdot 3.9927 = 4{,}591{,}605$; $NPV = 4{,}591{,}605 - 4{,}000{,}000 = 591{,}605$; $PI = 4{,}591{,}605 / 4{,}000{,}000 = 1.148$.

| Project | $I_0$ (€) | $PV$ (€) | NPV (€) | PI | PI rank |
|:--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--:|
| A | 4,000,000 | 4,591,605 | 591,605 | 1.148 | 2 |
| B | 2,500,000 | 3,034,452 | 534,452 | 1.214 | 1 |
| C | 3,500,000 | 3,992,700 | 492,700 | 1.141 | 3 |
| D | 1,500,000 | 1,676,934 | 176,934 | 1.118 | 4 |
| E | 6,000,000 | 6,388,320 | 388,320 | 1.065 | 5 |

All PIs exceed 1, so every project creates value on its own. PI ranking: **B, A, C, D, E**. (With the exact factor 3.99271, the results differ by at most a few euros.)
:::

#### Task 2: Filling €6.0 million

Fill the €6.0 million budget with the PI procedure. Compare the result with the rule "highest NPV first, as long as it fits".

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

*PI procedure* (B, A, C, D, E): B (€2.5 million, €3.5 million left) → A (€4.0 million) does not fit, skip → C (€3.5 million, nothing left). Portfolio **B + C**:

$$NPV_{B+C} = 534{,}452 + 492{,}700 = 1{,}027{,}152$$

*Highest NPV first* (A, B, C, E, D): A (€4.0 million, €2.0 million left) → B, C, E do not fit → D (€1.5 million, €0.5 million left). Portfolio **A + D**, €0.5 million idle:

$$NPV_{A+D} = 591{,}605 + 176{,}934 = 768{,}539$$

The PI portfolio creates **€258,613 more** value with the same budget. A has the largest NPV but uses up two thirds of the budget and blocks the two efficient mid-sized projects — the elephant trap. (Enumeration of all combinations confirms B + C as the optimum for €6.0 million.)
:::

#### Task 3: Check the margin

After a renegotiation, the banks allow **€7.5 million**. Apply the PI procedure again. Is the result optimal? If not, find a better portfolio and explain why the PI ranking missed it.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

*PI procedure:* B (€5.0 million left) → A (€1.0 million left) → C (€3.5 million) and D (€1.5 million) do not fit → E does not fit. Portfolio **B + A**, outlay €6.5 million, **€1.0 million idle**:

$$NPV_{A+B} = 534{,}452 + 591{,}605 = 1{,}126{,}057$$

*Margin check:* the idle €1.0 million plus A's €4.0 million equal exactly C + D ($3.5 + 1.5 = 5.0$ million). Replace A by C and D: portfolio **B + C + D**, outlay $2.5 + 3.5 + 1.5 = 7.5$ million (budget fully used):

$$NPV_{B+C+D} = 534{,}452 + 492{,}700 + 176{,}934 = 1{,}204{,}086$$

That is **€78,029 more** than the PI selection, and the optimum by enumeration. The PI ranking is exact only for divisible projects; with indivisible projects, a high-ranked project (A) can leave a gap that no remaining project fills, so a combination of lower-ranked projects that uses the whole budget can create more total NPV.

**Grading Notes:** full marks require the identification of idle capital as the warning sign and the comparison of the two portfolios' total NPVs.
:::

## Exercise 3: Concepts and Limits

#### Task 1: Multiple choice — capital rationing

Which of the following statements are **correct**? (Multiple answers possible.)

a) In the Dean model, projects are sorted by IRR in descending order and financing sources by cost in ascending order.

b) The endogenous cut-off rate always equals the IRR of the last accepted project.

c) A project with a PI of 1.25 has an NPV equal to 25% of its initial outlay.

d) Without a budget constraint, the PI rule accepts exactly the same projects as the NPV rule.

e) Under a fixed budget, ranking projects by absolute NPV maximises the total NPV of the portfolio.

f) Soft capital rationing is imposed by banks and the capital market.

g) All statements are false.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:** Correct are **a)**, **c)** and **d)**.

- **a) Correct.** This is the construction of the investment and the financing staircase.
- **b) Incorrect.** That holds only when the staircases cross on a vertical step of the financing staircase. If they cross on a vertical step of the investment staircase, the cut-off rate is the cost of the marginal financing source (Exercise 1, Task 4).
- **c) Correct.** $PI = 1 + NPV / I_0$, so $NPV / I_0 = 1.25 - 1 = 0.25$.
- **d) Correct.** $PI > 1$ is equivalent to $NPV > 0$.
- **e) Incorrect.** Ranking by NPV favours large projects and can crowd out more efficient smaller ones (Exercise 2, Task 2).
- **f) Incorrect.** Soft rationing is imposed by management itself; limits imposed by banks or the capital market are hard rationing.
- **g) Incorrect**, since a), c) and d) are correct.
:::

#### Task 2: Transfer — a budget for two years

A division of Morgenrot receives **€2.0 million** at $t = 0$ and another **€1.0 million** at $t = 1$; unused money cannot be carried forward. Four independent, indivisible projects compete for it (€ million; NPVs at the cost of capital):

| Project | Outlay $t = 0$ | Outlay $t = 1$ | NPV |
|:--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Q | 1.0 | 1.0 | 0.50 |
| S | 1.0 | 0 | 0.30 |
| T | 1.0 | 0 | 0.25 |
| R | 0 | 1.0 | 0.40 |

a) Which portfolio does the PI ranking (based on the outlay at $t = 0$) select, and what is its total NPV?

b) Find a portfolio that respects both budgets and creates more NPV.

c) Explain in two or three sentences why the PI ranking fails here and which method gives the correct answer.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show_solutions"}
**Solution:**

**a)** $PI = 1 + NPV / I_0$: Q $= 1.50$, S $= 1.30$, T $= 1.25$; R has no outlay at $t = 0$ and cannot be ranked. The PI ranking selects **Q + S** ($t = 0$: 2.0; $t = 1$: 1.0), total NPV $0.50 + 0.30 = 0.80$, i.e. **€0.80 million**.

**b)** **S + T + R** uses €2.0 million at $t = 0$ and €1.0 million at $t = 1$ and creates $0.30 + 0.25 + 0.40 = 0.95$, i.e. **€0.95 million** — €0.15 million more. (Q + R would need €2.0 million at $t = 1$ and is infeasible; Q + T yields only €0.75 million.)

**c)** The PI divides by the outlay at $t = 0$ only, so it does not see that Q also consumes the entire budget of $t = 1$ — a resource that R would use more profitably — and it cannot rank R at all. When budgets bind in several periods, the projects must be compared as complete combinations against all budget constraints: for a few projects by enumerating all feasible combinations, for larger problems by (integer) linear programming.

**Grading Notes:** for c), the key point is that a single ratio based on $I_0$ ignores claims on later budgets; naming enumeration or mathematical programming as the remedy completes the answer.
:::
